newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-TRADE QUESTION: WILL CHANGES IN LATITUDE CHANGE ATTITUDES?.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-TRADE QUESTION: WILL CHANGES IN LATITUDE CHANGE ATTITUDES?.

text.p: "Changes in latitude, changes in attitude" was the hopeful theme song of the NBA trading season as two bad teams swapped a slew of problem personalities, but the elite clubs mostly stood pat.
The trade deadline passed Thursday night with a flurry of minor deals on the heels of a blockbuster. However, only two top title contenders have made even one small tweak recently.
The Chicago Bulls -- favoured to win their fifth championship of the Michael Jordan era -- made no changes. Why should they, as long as they have Jordan?

Miami coach/general manager Pat Riley's Heat, with the second-best record in the NBA, added small forward Jamal Mashburn to centre Alonzo Mourning and guard Tim Hardaway, capitalising on Don Nelson's demolition and reconstruction of the bickering Dallas Mavericks.
Third best in the league, the Detroit Pistons were content to keep on watching the growth of the latest and greatest "next Jordan," Grant Hill.

Soaking up savvy from teammate Joe Dumars and spurred into nastier spirit by coach Doug Collins, Hill recently surprised a Madison Square Garden crowd by returning a fan's obscenity in kind after pounding a series of one-on-one drives down the New York Knicks' throats.
No more Goody Two-Shoes, no more Mr Nice Guy, the tough New York fans murmured appreciatively.

The Knicks, who wound up winning that battle, likewise made no trades, encouraged by the progress of the three new starters placed around Patrick Ewing this season: Allan Houston, Larry Johnson and Chris Childs.

In the Western Conference, after injuries to centre Shaquille O'Neal and recently acquired forward Robert Horry, the Los Angeles Lakers picked up swingman George McCloud from the revamped New Jersey Nets to help hold the fort.
Elden Campbell and rookie Travis Knight, drafted and quickly cast off by the Bulls, were already doing a passable job making up for O'Neal's absence.

The sputtering Seattle SuperSonics, last year's runner-ups led by Shawn Kemp and Gary Payton, tampered with their chemistry coming into this season but stayed out of the laboratory come trading time, and despite their unhappiness remained right behind the Lakers in the standings.

The Houston Rockets have been busy at the medicine cabinet trying to keep veteran superstars Hakeem Olajuwon, Charles Barkley and Clyde Drexler healthy, but sought no midseason injections of fresh talent. Neither did another vintage team, the Utah Jazz of John Stockton and Karl Malone.

The two above-mentioned changes -- Mashburn and McCloud -- were prelude and postscript to the blockbuster deal in which Nelson finished cleaning out what he called the "mess" in Dallas by exchanging nine players with the Nets. Not one of last year's Mavericks remains with Dallas.
Both new-look teams were in action Thursday night and both lost, but more respectably than they had grown used to.

In a five-point loss to Miami, the Nets' new point guard Sam Cassell equalled the team high with 17 points, new centre Eric Montross had 12 points and 11 rebounds (but looked immobile on defence) and All-Star forward Chris Gatling had 13 points and 10 rebounds.
Only guard Jimmy Jackson, expected to have the biggest future of them all, was off, shooting 2-for-9 for five points. Backup centre Joe Kleine was still on his way from the Lakers.
"I think we got a lot better overnight," said the Nets' Kendall Gill. Coach John Calipari, brought in with sweeping powers this season to "The Swamp" in New Jersey, was giddy.

Now he had players who could score without him calling a set play on every possession, he exulted -- and he also could look forward to up to $14 million (likely much less) in salary cap room in two years, along with a couple of draft picks.
"I went for a run today and I ran faster than I have in a year and a half," the rookie NBA coach said.
Calipari rolled the dice with the deal, but Nelson's gamble looked to be much the greater.

Already scarred by sour relations with players in New York and Golden State, Nelson was leaning on the ultra-slim reed of Shawn Bradley, at 7 feet, 6 inches (2.29 metres) the second tallest man in NBA history but more devoted to his family and religion than to the sport genetics thrust upon him.
The Mavericks also picked up unhappy guards Robert Pack and Khalid Reeves and little-used forward Ed O'Bannon.

Bradley had 10 points, 10 rebounds and six blocks despite feeling like "a lost sheep" in his Dallas debut, a two-point loss to the Milwaukee Bucks. Pack sat out the game with an ankle sprain and Reeves scored eight points before leaving with an injury.
Sweet-shooting Sasha Danilovic, acquired from Miami in the Mashburn deal, was not with the Mavericks for the game.

Point guard Mark Jackson, the NBA assists leader, headlined a six-player trade Thursday when he was sent back to Indiana with centre LaSalle Thompson and rookie forward Darvin Ham for swingman Vincent Askew, guard Jerome Allen and forward Eddie Johnson, plus second-round draft picks in 1997 and 1998.
Guard Ricky Pierce was part of another Denver trade, gave the Charlotte Hornets added depth when he was dealt for guard Anthony Goldwire and centre George Zidek.
